lessons.title: Identifying and scoring vulnerabilities
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a magnifying glass on a brick wall; a cracked brick is circled in red with a "CVE" label.
objectives: Tell apart vulnerability, threat, exploit and weakness (CVE and CWE).
Read a CVSS score and know its limits.
Use public sources: NVD, the KEV catalog, the EPSS score, vendor advisories.
Choose a suitable type of scan and frame it with an authorization.

references.title: FIRST, Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v3.1 and v4.0
NIST SP 800-115, Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

blocks.text: What are we talking about?

rows: Exploitable weakness in a system, software or process
A VPN version that accepts a malformed request
A criminal group that targets VPNs
Code or technique that actually exploits the vulnerability
A public script that gives access without a password

blocks.title: CVE, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures
blocks.text: Unique, public identifier of a specific vulnerability, in the form CVE-year-number. It lets everyone (vendors, scanners, SOCs) talk about the same flaw.

blocks.title: CWE, Common Weakness Enumeration
blocks.text: Catalog of TYPES of weaknesses (SQL injection, buffer overflow…). A CVE is a concrete case; the CWE is the family it belongs to.
"CVE = the case, CWE = the family, CVSS = the severity."
Scoring severity: CVSS

CVSS, published by FIRST, gives a score from 0 to 10 based on technical criteria: attack vector (network, local, physical), complexity, privileges required, user interaction and impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability.

blocks.title: CVSS measures severity, not risk
blocks.text: The base score knows nothing about your asset, its exposure or whether real attacks exist. A 9.8 flaw on an isolated test workstation can be less urgent than a 7.5 flaw on an Internet-facing server that is being actively exploited.
Sources to watch

blocks.title: From disclosure to the scanner alert
blocks.alt: Five-step diagram: a researcher or a vendor discovers the flaw, a CVE identifier is assigned, the NVD enriches it with a CVSS score, the vendor publishes an advisory and a patch, then scanners add a detection test.

rows: Public database of enriched CVEs: CVSS score, affected products, references
List of vulnerabilities whose real-world exploitation is confirmed
Estimated probability that a CVE will be exploited in the next 30 days

blocks.text: Scanning your systems

blocks.title: Four ways to scan
blocks.alt: Two-by-two grid. Unauthenticated scan: an attacker's view from the network, more false positives. Authenticated scan: logs into the system and sees installed versions, more accurate. Installed agent: ideal for mobile workstations. Passive analysis: listens to traffic without sending anything, useful for fragile devices.

blocks.title: Scanning without authorization
blocks.text: A scan, even on your employer's network, must be authorized in writing, with a defined scope and schedule. Scanning a system that does not belong to you can be an offense. Some fragile devices (industrial controllers, medical equipment) can fail under an active scan.

A scanner finds KNOWN vulnerabilities. It replaces neither a penetration test, which tries to chain them as an attacker would, nor a configuration review. And it produces false positives: an analyst must validate before alerting the teams.

blocks.title: SOC case: the VPN in the KEV catalog
blocks.text: On Monday morning, the SOC's watch spots that a CVE affecting the company's VPN model has just entered the KEV catalog. The authorized authenticated scan confirms that two Internet-facing gateways run the vulnerable version. The SOC opens a priority ticket, searches the SIEM for traces of exploitation over the last 30 days (unusual requests, new accounts) and alerts the network team for an emergency patch.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: I want a complete inventory; a vulnerability on an unknown asset will never be fixed.
SOC manager: watching KEV and vendor advisories feeds my compromise hunts directly.
Auditor: I check scan coverage, frequency and written authorization.
Risk manager: I turn a vulnerability into a risk by adding the exposure and criticality of the asset.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: CVE = identifier of a specific flaw; CWE = type of weakness; CVSS = severity score.
The CVSS base score is not a risk level: it ignores the company's context.
Authenticated scan = more accurate, fewer false positives; unauthenticated = attacker's view.
A vulnerability scan is not a penetration test.
Always a written authorization and a scope before scanning.
Vulnerability, threat, exploit, risk: four distinct concepts.
CVE, CWE and CVSS (0 to 10; 7 to 8.9 high; 9 to 10 critical).
Sources: NVD, KEV (confirmed exploitation), EPSS (probability), vendor advisories.
Authenticated, unauthenticated, agent-based or passive scans, always authorized.

lessons.title: Prioritizing and treating vulnerabilities
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of three sorting trays marked "now", "soon" and "later", with red, orange and green vulnerability cards.
objectives: Prioritize by risk: severity, exploitation, exposure and asset criticality.
Choose between fixing, mitigating and accepting by exception.
Steer the program with deadlines (SLAs) and indicators.

blocks.text: A cycle, not a scan

blocks.title: The vulnerability management cycle
blocks.alt: Six-step cycle around the asset inventory: discover through scanning and watch, assess by validating and ruling out false positives, prioritize by risk, treat with a patch or mitigation, verify with a new scan, report with indicators.

blocks.text: Prioritizing by risk
A large company discovers thousands of vulnerabilities every month. Fixing everything at once is impossible. So several criteria are combined to deal first with what really matters.

blocks.title: The four prioritization questions
items: Severity: what is the CVSS score?
Exploitation: is it already exploited (KEV) or likely to be (high EPSS, public exploit)?
Exposure: is the asset reachable from the Internet or from a poorly protected segment?
Criticality: does the asset carry sensitive data or a vital process?

blocks.title: Where to place four vulnerabilities?
blocks.alt: Matrix with technical severity on the horizontal axis and probability of exploitation on the vertical axis. The exposed VPN listed in KEV is at the top right: to be treated immediately. The internal web server is in the middle. The critical flaw on an isolated test workstation is on the right but at the bottom. The printer with a low flaw is at the bottom left.

blocks.text: Treatment options

rows: A patch or a new version exists
Disable the vulnerable feature, filter the port, web application firewall rule (virtual patch)
Fix impossible in the short term, risk accepted
Certified industrial machine, isolated, reviewed every 6 months
Shut down an old forgotten server

blocks.title: Virtual patch (patch virtuel)
blocks.text: Measure placed in front of the vulnerable system (web application firewall, IPS, filter) that blocks exploitation without modifying the system itself. It is a temporary compensating control, not a fix.

blocks.title: An exception is managed like a risk
blocks.text: Every exception is written, justified, approved by the risk owner, backed by compensating controls and limited in time. Without a review date, an exception becomes an oversight.
Steering the program

rows: Mean time to remediate by severity
Whether the set deadlines (SLAs) are met
Share of critical vulnerabilities past due
The delay that is really dangerous
Number of active and expired exceptions
Fixes that were badly done or incomplete

blocks.text: "Severity, Exploitation, Exposure, Stakes": the 4 criteria that turn a score into a priority.

Remediation deadlines are set by the company's policy, often shorter for critical or exploited flaws. There is no universal deadline imposed by the exam: remember the logic (the higher the risk, the shorter the deadline) rather than a figure.

blocks.title: SOC case: the forgotten exception
blocks.text: While preparing the monthly report, the L2 analyst notices a critical vulnerability open for 14 months on a monitoring server. An exception had been granted for 3 months, during a migration that never happened. The SOC alerts the CISO; the risk owner has to choose: fix, renew the exception with new compensating controls, or retire the server. Meanwhile, the SOC adds a specific detection rule on this server.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: I do not ask for zero vulnerabilities; I ask that exposed critical ones be treated on time.
Operations: a poorly tested urgent patch can cause an outage; I want a realistic deadline and a rollback.
Auditor: I check that every exception has an owner, a justification and an expiry date.
SOC analyst: an unpatched vulnerability on an exposed asset deserves closer monitoring.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Prioritize by risk, not only by CVSS score.
A virtual patch is a compensating, temporary measure, not a fix.
An exception is approved by the risk owner, not by the analyst nor the administrator.
After fixing, you VERIFY with a new scan.
The cycle relies on the asset inventory.
Cycle: discover, assess, prioritize, treat, verify, report.
Priority = severity + exploitation (KEV, EPSS) + exposure + asset criticality.
Treat: fix, mitigate (virtual patch), accept by limited exception, retire.
Indicators: deadlines by severity, critical past due, coverage, exceptions.

lessons.title: Patch management and security testing
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a computer screen with a large cross-shaped bandage and a circular update arrow.
objectives: Apply a patch management process, from testing to deployment in waves.
React to a zero-day vulnerability and manage end-of-life systems.
Tell apart vulnerability scan, penetration test, audit and Red Team exercise.

references.title: NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 4, Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning
NIST SP 800-115, Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

blocks.text: The patching process

blocks.title: From published patch to verified patch
blocks.alt: Six-step diagram: watch for published patches, assessment of their relevance and urgency, testing on a representative environment, deployment in waves with a rollback plan, verification of installation, inventory update and closure.

blocks.text: Patch management is part of change management: a patch is a change, with impact analysis, approval and a rollback plan. Routine patches can be pre-approved (standard change); an urgent patch follows the emergency change procedure.

blocks.title: Deploying in waves (share of the estate)
blocks.alt: Bar chart: the pilot wave covers 5% of the estate with volunteer users and IT, the first wave 20%, the general wave 75%. You move to the next wave only if the previous one caused no problem.

blocks.title: Good practices
items: Keep a complete software inventory, including firmware, libraries and third-party applications.
Download patches only from official sources and check their signature.
Plan a rollback and a backup before major updates.
Verify after deployment: a "distributed" patch is not necessarily "installed" (missing reboot, silent failure).

blocks.text: The hard cases

blocks.title: Zero-day vulnerability
blocks.text: Vulnerability exploited or known before a patch exists. You can only mitigate: disable the feature, filter, isolate, strengthen detection, then apply the patch as soon as it is published.

blocks.title: End-of-life system, EOL (système en fin de vie)
blocks.text: System for which the vendor no longer publishes security patches. Every new flaw will stay open: it must be replaced, or isolated with compensating controls and a formal exception in the meantime.

blocks.title: The patch that breaks production
blocks.text: A patch applied everywhere at once, without testing, can stop a critical service. Conversely, waiting too long leaves the door open. Deployment in waves and rollback make it possible to move fast without risking everything.
Testing security: four approaches

rows: Prove that flaws can be exploited and pushed further
Manual, signed scope and rules of engagement, one-off
Test detection and response against a realistic scenario
Stealthy, over time, with the defense team (Blue Team) put to the test

blocks.title: Rules of engagement
blocks.text: A penetration test is only legal and safe if it is authorized in writing by the owner of the systems: scope, dates, allowed and prohibited techniques, emergency contacts, handling of the data discovered. Without this document, it is an attack.
"The scan lists, the pentest proves, the audit compares, the Red Team tests the defense."

Black, gray or white box: what changes is the information given to the tester. In a black box the tester knows nothing (like an external attacker), in a white box they have everything (code, diagrams, accounts), in a gray box part of it, often a user account.

blocks.title: SOC case: the Friday-night zero-day
blocks.text: A vendor announces an actively exploited flaw in its mail server, with no patch available for several days, but with a workaround. The SOC triggers the "zero-day" playbook: the workaround is applied as an emergency change, external access is filtered, the published indicators of compromise are searched for in the logs, monitoring is strengthened. The patch, published on Tuesday, is tested then deployed in two waves; an authenticated scan confirms the installation.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: an end-of-life system is a risk that grows every month; I want a dated replacement plan.
Operations: I pre-approve routine patches to keep the urgent path for real emergencies.
Auditor: I compare the publication date of critical patches with their installation date.
SOC manager: during a zero-day, detection makes up for the missing patch.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: A patch is a change: it goes through change management.
Zero-day = no patch: you mitigate and monitor.
Scan ≠ penetration test ≠ audit ≠ Red Team.
A penetration test requires written authorization and rules of engagement.
Verify the installation: distributed does not mean installed.
Patches: watch, assessment, test, deployment in waves with rollback, verification.
Zero-day: mitigate, isolate, detect; EOL: replace or isolate with an exception.
Scan (list), penetration test (proof), audit (compliance), Red Team (detection and response).
Always a written authorization and rules of engagement.

questions.prompt: What is a vulnerability?
choices: The amount of an expected annual loss
An exploitable weakness in a system or process
A malicious person seeking to cause harm
A patch published by the software vendor
questions.explanation: The vulnerability is the weakness; the threat is what can exploit it.

whyNot.0: That is a financial measure of risk (ALE).
whyNot.2: A malicious person is a threat source.
whyNot.3: The patch is what removes the vulnerability.

questions.prompt: What is a CVE identifier used for?
choices: Classifying the main types of weaknesses
Uniquely identifying a specific vulnerability
Encrypting the scan reports that are exchanged
Rating the technical severity of a flaw
questions.explanation: A CVE (CVE-year-number) lets everyone talk about the same vulnerability.

whyNot.0: Types of weaknesses are classified by the CWE.
whyNot.2: The CVE has no encryption role.
whyNot.3: Severity is given by the CVSS.

questions.prompt: "SQL injection" corresponds to which concept?
choices: A type of weakness listed in the CWE
An entry in the CISA KEV catalog
A CVSS technical severity score
A CVE identifier assigned to a product
questions.explanation: The CWE classifies families of weaknesses; a CVE is a concrete case in a given product.

whyNot.1: The KEV lists exploited CVEs, not types of weaknesses.
whyNot.2: The CVSS is a numerical score.
whyNot.3: A CVE identifies a specific flaw in a product, not a family.

questions.prompt: With CVSS v3.1, which severity matches a score of 9.1?
choices: Medium
Low
High
Critical
questions.explanation: 9.0 to 10.0 = critical; 7.0 to 8.9 = high; 4.0 to 6.9 = medium; 0.1 to 3.9 = low.

whyNot.0: Medium ranges from 4.0 to 6.9.
whyNot.1: Low ranges from 0.1 to 3.9.

questions.prompt: Why is the CVSS base score not enough to prioritize a fix?
choices: It changes every day and is therefore not stable enough to decide on
It ignores exposure, asset criticality and actual exploitation
It is confidential and reserved for the vendor of the software concerned
It only applies to password-related vulnerabilities
questions.explanation: The CVSS base score measures technical severity; priority also depends on the company's context and the actual threat.

whyNot.0: The base score is stable; that is not the problem.
whyNot.3: The CVSS applies to every type of software vulnerability.

questions.prompt: What does the KEV catalog published by CISA contain?
choices: The monthly patches published by Microsoft
The default passwords of network devices
Every vulnerability published worldwide
Vulnerabilities whose real-world exploitation is confirmed
questions.explanation: KEV = Known Exploited Vulnerabilities: flaws that are already exploited, and therefore a priority.

whyNot.0: The KEV covers all vendors and does not distribute patches.
whyNot.1: It is not a list of passwords.
whyNot.2: That would be the NVD; the KEV keeps only a small part of it.

questions.prompt: What does the EPSS score measure?
choices: The number of assets in the fleet affected by the flaw
The estimated probability that a CVE will be exploited in the next 30 days
The average time the company takes to fix a flaw
The technical severity of a flaw, from 0 to 10
questions.explanation: EPSS, published by FIRST, complements the CVSS with an estimate of the probability of exploitation.

whyNot.0: EPSS knows nothing about your fleet.
whyNot.2: Time to fix is an internal indicator.
whyNot.3: Technical severity is measured by the CVSS.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of an authenticated scan?
choices: It does not require any authorization from the owner of the systems
It replaces a targeted manual penetration test
It sees the versions actually installed and produces fewer false positives
It is invisible to the SOC and leaves no trace
questions.explanation: Logged on to the system, the scanner reads versions and configurations instead of guessing them from the network.

whyNot.0: Every scan must be authorized.
whyNot.1: It lists the flaws but does not exploit them.
whyNot.3: A scan must be known to the SOC, not hidden.

questions.prompt: Before launching a vulnerability scan, which elements are essential? (2 answers)
choices: A defined scope and time window
Disabling the SIEM during the scan
The scanner vendor's approval
Written authorization from the owner of the systems
questions.explanation: The scan is authorized, bounded and scheduled; the SOC is warned so that it does not mistake the scan for an attack.

whyNot.1: The SOC is warned; monitoring is not disabled.
whyNot.2: The scanner vendor does not need to authorize your scans.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between a vulnerability scan and a penetration test?
choices: There is no difference: they are two names for the same activity
Unlike the scan, the penetration test does not require authorization
The scan lists the flaws; the penetration test exploits them
The scan is always manual, the penetration test always automated
questions.explanation: The scan is automated and broad; the penetration test is manual, targeted and demonstrates exploitation.

whyNot.0: The goals and methods differ.
whyNot.1: The penetration test requires written authorization.
whyNot.3: The scan is usually automated.

questions.prompt: Which step follows remediation in the vulnerability management cycle?
choices: Buying a new scanner
Verification by a new scan
Deleting the logs
Discovery
questions.explanation: You check that the fix is effective before closing.

whyNot.0: Changing tools is not a step in the cycle.
whyNot.3: Discovery opens the cycle.

questions.prompt: Which vulnerability should be handled FIRST?
choices: CVSS 5.0 on an internal printer
CVSS 8.1 on an Internet-facing VPN gateway, listed in the KEV
CVSS 3.1 on a development server
CVSS 9.8 on an isolated test workstation, with no known exploit
questions.explanation: An actively exploited flaw on an exposed asset carries the highest risk, even if its score is a little lower.

whyNot.0: Medium severity on a low-criticality internal asset.
whyNot.3: High score, but an isolated asset and no exploitation: lower risk.

questions.prompt: Which criteria, besides the CVSS, go into risk-based prioritization? (2 answers)
choices: Evidence or probability of exploitation (KEV, EPSS)
The number of letters in the server's name
The exposure of the asset (Internet, poorly protected segment)
The color of the scanner's interface
questions.explanation: Exposure, exploitation and asset criticality turn a technical score into a priority.

whyNot.1: A server's name has no link to risk.
whyNot.3: The interface has no link to risk.

questions.prompt: What is a virtual patch?
choices: A patch installed only in a virtual machine
A remediation exception granted with no end date
A WAF or IPS rule that blocks exploitation without touching the system
A patch downloaded from an unofficial site
questions.explanation: The virtual patch is a temporary compensating measure while waiting for the real fix.

whyNot.0: The word "virtual" does not refer to virtualization here.
whyNot.1: An exception with no date is bad practice.
whyNot.3: That is a risk, not a security measure.

questions.prompt: Who must approve a remediation exception for a critical vulnerability?
choices: The (business) risk owner, with the advice of security
The vendor of the vulnerability scanner
Any system administrator on the team
The analyst who found the flaw during the scan
questions.explanation: Accepting a risk is the job of the person accountable for it, informed by security.

whyNot.1: The vendor has no authority over your risks.
whyNot.2: The administrator implements; they do not own the business risk.
whyNot.3: The analyst reports; they do not decide to accept the risk.

questions.prompt: Which elements must a well-managed remediation exception include? (2 answers)
choices: An expiration or review date
Stopping the scans on this asset
Removing the asset from the inventory
Compensating measures
questions.explanation: The exception is justified, compensated and limited in time.

whyNot.1: Scanning continues in order to track the risk.
whyNot.2: Removing the asset from the inventory would make it invisible.

questions.prompt: An old, forgotten server no longer serves any purpose and has critical vulnerabilities. What is the best option?
choices: Raise its CVSS score
Hide it in another network without saying so
Decommission it
Accept it
questions.explanation: A useless system is decommissioned: it is the safest and cheapest way to remove the risk.

whyNot.0: The score changes nothing about the risk.
whyNot.1: A hidden, unmanaged system remains a risk.
whyNot.3: Accepting a pointless risk makes no sense.

questions.prompt: Which indicator best reveals a dangerous delay in remediation?
choices: The total number of vulnerabilities found by the scans
The number of scanners bought and deployed in the year
The share of critical vulnerabilities not fixed within the set deadline
The average size of the scan reports sent to the teams
questions.explanation: Missed deadlines on critical flaws measure the risk actually left open.

whyNot.0: The total depends mainly on the size of the fleet and on coverage.
whyNot.1: The number of tools is not a result.
whyNot.3: The size of a report is not a risk indicator.

questions.prompt: The scanner reports a critical flaw on a server, but the team says it applied a patch backported by the vendor without changing the version number. What should be done?
choices: Close the alert without checking, since the team says so
Delete the scanner's detection rule for all the servers in the fleet
Check that the patch is present before concluding it is a false positive
Reinstall the server immediately from a fresh image
questions.explanation: A false positive is demonstrated with evidence; it is documented, then tuned.

whyNot.0: Closing without evidence can leave a real flaw open.
whyNot.1: Deleting the rule everywhere would hide real cases.
whyNot.3: Reinstalling is disproportionate before checking.

questions.prompt: What is every vulnerability management program built on?
choices: Trust in the vendors
A single annual scan
An up-to-date asset inventory
Buying a firewall
questions.explanation: You can neither scan nor fix an asset you do not know about.

whyNot.0: Trust does not replace verification.
whyNot.1: An annual scan leaves months of flaws invisible.
whyNot.3: A firewall does not replace vulnerability management.

questions.prompt: Why test a patch before deploying it across the whole fleet?
choices: Because patches are always malicious
To check that it does not break a critical service
To delay the fix as long as possible
Because the law prohibits patches
questions.explanation: Testing limits the risk of an outage; it must remain proportionate to the urgency.

whyNot.0: Official patches are not malicious, but their source must be checked.
whyNot.2: Testing must not be used as an excuse for delay.
whyNot.3: No law prohibits patches.

questions.prompt: A zero-day flaw is being exploited and no patch exists. Which response is the most appropriate?
choices: Wait for the patch to be published without changing anything
Publish the flaw on social media to raise the alarm
Work around, filter or isolate, and strengthen detection
Uninstall the antivirus to avoid conflicts
questions.explanation: Without a patch, you reduce exposure and monitor until the patch is published.

whyNot.0: Doing nothing leaves the door open.
whyNot.1: That is not a protective measure.
whyNot.3: That would reduce protection.

questions.prompt: An operating system is no longer maintained by its vendor (end of life). What is the main risk?
choices: It becomes faster
It can no longer be backed up
New flaws will no longer be fixed
It loses its keyboard license
questions.explanation: Without patches, every new flaw stays open: replace it, or isolate it with compensating measures.

whyNot.0: End of life has no effect on speed.
whyNot.1: Backups remain possible.
whyNot.3: That is not a real effect.

questions.prompt: Which elements reduce the risk of a patch deployment? (2 answers)
choices: Deploying to the whole fleet at once without testing
Deleting backups to free up space
Deploying in waves, starting with a pilot group
A tested rollback plan
questions.explanation: Waves and rollback let you move fast without risking everything.

whyNot.0: A problem would hit the whole fleet at once.
whyNot.1: Backups are the last safety net if something fails.

questions.prompt: How should an urgent patch be handled with respect to change management?
choices: It is applied by any administrator, with no record
It is completely exempt from the change management process
It waits for the next monthly change board meeting
It follows the emergency change procedure, recorded and reviewed
questions.explanation: A patch is a change; urgency speeds up the process without removing it.

whyNot.0: The lack of a record prevents oversight and investigation.
whyNot.1: No change is exempt from the process.
whyNot.2: Waiting a month would be too long for an emergency.

questions.prompt: After a patch has been deployed, what must be done?
choices: Erase the installation logs to free up space
Close the ticket without any further check
Disable automatic updates on the workstations
Check that it is actually installed and that the vulnerability is gone
questions.explanation: A distributed patch is not necessarily installed (failure, missing restart).

whyNot.0: The logs serve as evidence.
whyNot.1: Without verification, the flaw may remain open.

questions.prompt: Which exercise is mainly intended to test the defense team's ability to detect and respond?
choices: A Red Team exercise
A vulnerability scan
A policy review
A compliance audit
questions.explanation: The Red Team simulates a realistic, stealthy adversary to test the Blue Team.

whyNot.1: The scan lists known flaws.
whyNot.2: A policy review is a document review.
whyNot.3: The audit compares against a framework.

questions.prompt: A tester receives the source code, the network diagrams and accounts. What type of test is this?
choices: Gray box
Blind test
Black box
White box
questions.explanation: In a white-box test, the tester has all the information.

whyNot.0: In a gray-box test, they have part of it (often an account).
whyNot.1: A blind test gives little or no information.
whyNot.2: In a black-box test, they know nothing.

questions.prompt: Which elements must appear in the rules of engagement of a penetration test? (2 answers)
choices: The director's personal password
Permission to test the company's customers without their consent
Emergency contacts and prohibited techniques
The authorized scope and dates
questions.explanation: The rules of engagement set the limits of the test: what, when, how, and who to call if there is a problem.

whyNot.0: A personal secret is never handed over.
whyNot.1: Third-party systems can only be tested with their own authorization.

questions.prompt: Where should patches be downloaded from?
choices: From the vendor's official sources, checking their signature
From an attachment received by email
From a USB stick found in the parking lot
From an anonymous forum offering a faster version
questions.explanation: A fake patch is a classic vector for malware.

whyNot.1: An attachment is a phishing vector.
whyNot.2: A found USB stick is a classic attack vector.
whyNot.3: An anonymous source can distribute a trojanized file.
